newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian newspaper asks whether Yeltsin might quit.
newsitem.headline: Russian newspaper asks whether Yeltsin might quit.

text.p: A Russian newspaper on Saturday contemplated whether President Boris Yeltsin might consider stepping down for health reasons, fuelling debate over his ability to rule following heart surgery and now pneumonia.

"Regretfully, it is obvious that the president has no strength left to attend to affairs of the state properly," the liberal Komsomolskaya Pravda newspaper said of Yeltsin's struggle with pneumonia in hospital.

The 65-year-old president was taken to hospital on Wednesday and diagnosed as having pneumonia on Thursday. He faces almost a month more out of the Kremlin recovering, following an absence of of nearly half a year with heart trouble..

Komsomolskaya Pravda went on to ask what choice Yeltsin would now make. It said he would probably return to the Kremlin and continue to drive himself hard, but suggested there might now be other scenarios to consider.
"The first -- Yeltsin, weighing up his strength realistically, temporarily hands complete power to the prime minister for half a year," the popular daily said.
"The second -- Yeltsin opts for the boldest step of his life, something unprecedented in our rich history -- leaving the scene completely, honestly, calmly, with dignity."

Willingly giving up power seems out of character for Yeltsin, a man who has dedicated his life to gaining and keeping power, and who says he wants to be in a position to guarantee the reforms he has overseen are successful.
"He is first of all a man of power," former presidential press spokesman Vyacheslav Kostikov once said of Yeltsin. "Power is his ideology, his friend, his concubine, his mistress, his passion."
Declaring his candidacy for a second term last February, Yeltsin said he had unfinished business to complete.
"I have to bring to a successful end the matter to which I have fully devoted myself. I am sure that I can bring the country through turmoil, worries and uncertainty," he said.

Part of the business, preventing a return of communist rule in an election last year, is done. But other tasks, including guaranteeing reforms, remain unfinished because of his almost constant absence from the Kremlin for the last six months.
The odds are heavily against Yeltsin, a born fighter who is at his best when battling his way off the ropes, quitting even though he will be 66 on February 1.

But one of Yeltsin's doctors suggested on Friday that the president was depressed by his new health setback so soon afer his heart bypass operation on November 5, and by the blow it has dealt to his hopes of a vigorous second term in office.
"The man had just recovered from one very serious problem when a second one appeared, though it was a smaller one," Sergei Mironov, the chief Kremlin doctor, told reporters.
"Of course I cannot say Boris Nikolayevich feels comfortable spiritually. Of course this is depressing him, of course his mood is not a very happy one but I see no reason for particular pessimism."
Although Mironov said Yeltsin had, as usual, been resisting doctors' orders, any sign that his spirits are low is serious.
Komsomolskaya Pravda said that even if Yeltsin wanted to quit, others around him would persuade him to stay on for the sake of stability.

First among those would be Anatoly Chubais, the reformist head of the Kremlin administration who is anxious not to give his political foe, ousted security adviser Alexander Lebed, any chance to become president.
Yeltsin's wife Naina may be less happy for him to soldier on. She said in November 1995, that it would be better for his health if he did not seek a second term as president.
But she pointed out that Yeltsin had the final say on all matters and did not heed advice.
